children.translated_text: The ear is the āhaṃkārika sense faculty that apprehends sound.
Ākāśa, space, is the product of the subtle element of sound.
The relation between the two has the character of the relation of place and occupant.

children.text: tasmin kṛtasaṃyamasya yoginaḥ divyaṃ śrotraṃ pravartate yugapat sūkṣmavyavahitaviprakṛṣṭaśabdagrahaṇasamarthaṃ bhavatītyarthaḥ ||
children.translated_text: For the yogin who has performed <s>saṃyama</s> on that relation, divine hearing arises; that is, it becomes capable of apprehending at once sounds that are subtle, concealed, or far distant.
He states another siddhi.
The body is the five-elemental body.

children.text: tasya ākāśena avakāśadāyakena yaḥ sambandhaḥ tatra saṃyamaṃ vidhāya laghuni tūlādau yā samāpattis tanmayībhāvalakṣaṇā tāṃ vidhāya prāptātyantalaghubhāvo yogī prathamaṃ yathāruci jale saṃcaran krameṇorṇanābhajantujālena saṃcaramāṇa ādityaraśmibhiś ca viharan yatheṣṭamākāśe gacchati ||
children.translated_text: Having performed <s>saṃyama</s> on its relation with ākāśa, which grants room, and having effected an attainment with what is light, such as cotton, characterized by becoming identical with it, the yogin who has obtained extreme lightness first moves on water as he wishes; then, in due course, moving on a spider's web and roaming by means of the sun's rays, he goes through the sky at will.
He states another siddhi.

children.text: śarīrād bahir yā manasaḥ śarīranairapekṣyeṇa vṛttiḥ sā mahāvidehā nāma vigataśarīrāhaṃkāradārḍhyadvāreṇocyate ||
children.translated_text: That activity of the mind which is outside the body and independent of the body is called the great disembodied state, because it is spoken of through the absence of firmness in the egoism connected with the body.

children.text: tataḥ tasyāṃ kṛtāt saṃyamāt prakāśāvaraṇakṣayaḥ sāttvikasya cittasya yaḥ prakāśas tasya yadāvaraṇaṃ kleśakarmādi tasya kṣayaḥ pravilayo bhavati ||
children.translated_text: From the <s>saṃyama</s> performed on that, there is the destruction of the covering of illumination: the covering, such as afflictions and actions, of the illumination belonging to the sattvic mind comes to destruction, that is, dissolution.
This is the meaning.

children.text: śarīrāhaṃkāre sati yā manaso bahirvṛttiḥ sā kalpitetyucyate ||
children.translated_text: When bodily egoism exists, the outward activity of the mind is said to be imagined.

children.text: yadā punaḥ śarīrāhaṃkārabhāvaṃ parityajya svātantreṇa manaso vṛttiḥ sā akalpitā tasyāṃ saṃyamāt yoginaḥ sarve cittamalāḥ kṣīyante ||
children.translated_text: But when, after abandoning the state of bodily egoism, the activity of the mind operates independently, that is unimagined; from <s>saṃyama</s> on it, all the impurities of the yogin's mind are destroyed.

children.text: tadevaṃ pūrvāntaviṣayā aparāntaviṣayā madhyabhāvāśca siddhīḥ pratipādyānantaraṃ bhuvanajñānādirūpā bāhyāḥ kāyavyūhādirūpā ābhyantarāḥ parikarmaniṣpannabhūtāś ca maitryādiṣu balāni ityevamādyāḥ samādhyupayoginīś cāntaḥkaraṇabahiḥkaraṇalakṣaṇendriyabhāvāḥ prāṇādivāyubhāvāś ca siddhīś cittadārḍhyāya samādheḥ samāśvāsotpattaye pratipādya idānīṃ svadarśanopayogisabījanirbījasamādhisiddhaye vividhopāyapradarśanāyāha ||
children.translated_text: Thus, after teaching the siddhis whose objects are the previous limit, the later limit, and intermediate states; the external siddhis such as knowledge of the worlds; the internal ones such as the arrangement of the body; the powers in friendliness and the rest, which are accomplished as preparatory practices; and also the sense-faculty states, characterized by the inner instrument and the outer instruments, and the states of the vital airs beginning with prāṇa, all useful for samādhi and taught for strengthening the mind and producing confidence in samādhi, he now speaks in order to show various means for the accomplishment of seed-based and seedless samādhi useful for the direct vision of the self.

children.text: pañcānāṃ pṛthivyādīnāṃ bhūtānāṃ ye pañcāvasthāviśeṣarūpā dharmāḥ sthūlatvādayaḥ tatra kṛtasaṃyamasya bhūtajayaḥ bhavati bhūtāni vaśyānyasya bhavantītyarthaḥ ||
children.translated_text: When <s>saṃyama</s> has been performed on the qualities, such as grossness, which are particular forms of the five states of the five elements beginning with earth, mastery over the elements arises; that is, the elements become subject to him.

children.text: tathāhi bhūtānāṃ paridṛśyamānaṃ viśiṣṭākāravad rūpaṃ sthūlaṃ svarūpaṃ caiṣāṃ yathākramaṃ kāryaṃ gandhasnehoṣṇatāpreraṇāvakāśadānalakṣaṇam ||
children.translated_text: For example, the visible form of the elements, possessing a distinct shape, is gross; and their own nature, respectively, is their effect, characterized as odor, cohesion, heat, propulsion, and the giving of space.

children.text: sūkṣmaṃ tu yathākramaṃ bhūtānāṃ kāraṇatvena vyavasthitāni gandhāditanmātrāṇi ||
children.translated_text: The subtle, however, consists respectively of the subtle elements beginning with odor, established as the causes of the elements.
The inhering guṇas are observed everywhere as inhering in all things, in the forms of illumination, activity, and stability.
Purposefulness is precisely the power in those guṇas called the accomplishment of experience and liberation.

children.text: tadevaṃ bhūteṣu pañcasu uktalakṣaṇāvasthāpanneṣu pratyavasthaṃ saṃyamaṃ kurvan yogī bhūtajayī bhavati ||
children.translated_text: Thus, by performing <s>saṃyama</s> on each state of the five elements as they possess the states characterized above, the yogin becomes master of the elements.

children.text: tadyathā prathamaṃ sthūlarūpe saṃyamaṃ vidhāya tadanu sūkṣmarūpe ityevaṃ krameṇa tasya kṛtasaṃyamasya saṃkalpānuvidhāyinyo vatsānusāriṇya iva gāvo bhūtaprakṛtayo bhavanti ||
children.translated_text: For instance, first performing <s>saṃyama</s> on the gross form and then on the subtle form, and so on in sequence, for him who has performed <s>saṃyama</s>, the elemental natures follow his resolve, like cows following their calves.
He states the fruit of that very mastery over the elements.
Aṇimā is the attainment of the state of being atomic.
Laghimā is the attainment of lightness, like a mass of cotton.
Garimā is the attainment of heaviness.
Mahimā is the attainment of greatness, the power to touch the moon and other bodies with the tip of a finger.
Prākāmya is the non-obstruction of desire.
Lordship over the body and the inner instrument is īśitva.

children.text: sarvatra prabhaviṣṇutā vaśitvaṃ sarvāṇy eva bhūtāṇi anurāgitvāt taduktaṃ nātikrāmanti ||
children.translated_text: Power to prevail everywhere is vaśitva; because all beings are devoted to him, they do not transgress his command.

children.text: kāmāvasāyitvaṃ sarvatra kāmāvasāyo yasmin viṣaye'sya kāma icchā bhavati tasmin viṣaye yogino 'vasāyo bhavati taṃ viṣayaṃ svīkāradvāreṇābhilāṣasamāptiparyantaṃ nayatītyarthaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Kāmāvasāyitva is the settling of desire everywhere: in whatever object he has desire, the yogin's determination occurs with regard to that object, meaning that, by taking possession of that object, he carries it through to the completion of his wish.

children.text: tatra te aṇimādyāḥ samādhyupayogino bhūtajayāt yoginaḥ prādurbhavanti ||
children.translated_text: There, those siddhis beginning with aṇimā, useful for samādhi, appear for the yogin from mastery over the elements.
For example, having attained atomic size, he enters even inside diamonds and the like.
This should be applied everywhere in the same way.
These eight qualities beginning with aṇimā are called the great siddhis.
He obtains the bodily perfection that will be described.

children.text: taddharmānabhighātaś ca tasya kāyasya ye dharmā rūpādayasteṣāmabhighāto nāśo nāsya kutaścid api bhavati ||
children.translated_text: And there is no injury by its properties: the properties of that body, such as color and the rest, are not injured or destroyed for him by anything at all.

children.text: nāsya rūpamagnirdahati na ca vāyuḥ śoṣayati ityādi yojyam ||
children.translated_text: This is to be applied as: fire does not burn his form, nor does wind dry it up, and so on.
He states bodily perfection.
Beauty of form, grace, and strength are well known.

children.text: vajrasaṃhananaṃ vajravat kaṭhinā saṃhatirasya śarīre bhavatītyarthaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Adamantine compactness means that in his body there is a firm compactness like a diamond.
Thus there is the wealth of qualities manifested in the body.
Having thus described mastery over the elements, he states mastery over the senses for one who has reached that stage.
Grasping is the activity of the senses directed toward their objects.
Its own form, in general terms, is the capacity to illuminate.
<s>asmitā</s> is the following of egoity.
In the state of having no accumulation, it is as before.

children.text: eteṣāmindriyāṇāmavasthāpañcake pūrvavat saṃyamaṃ kṛtvā indriyajayī bhavati ||
children.translated_text: Having performed <s>saṃyama</s> on these senses in the five states as before, one becomes master of the senses.
He states its fruit.
<s>manojavitva</s>, swiftness like the mind, is the body's attainment of unsurpassed movement like that of the mind.
<s>vikaraṇabhāva</s> is the attainment of activity by the senses independently of the body.
Mastery over all is conquest of <s>pradhāna</s>.
These siddhis become manifest for one who has conquered the senses.
And in this śāstra they are called <s>madhupratīkā</s>.

children.text: yathā madhuna ekadeśo 'pi svadate evaṃ pratyekam etāḥ siddhayaḥ svadanta iti madhupratīkāḥ ||
children.translated_text: Just as even a single portion of honey is sweet, so each of these siddhis is sweet; therefore they are <s>madhupratīkā</s>.
Having described conquest of the senses, he states conquest of the inner organ.

children.text: tasmin śuddhe sāttvike pariṇāme kṛtasaṃyamasya yā sattvapuruṣayor utpadyate vivekakhyātiḥ sā anyatākhyātiḥ ||
children.translated_text: When that pure, sāttvika transformation has been made the object of <s>saṃyama</s>, the discriminative discernment that arises between <s>sattva</s> and <s>puruṣa</s> is the cognition of their difference.

children.text: guṇānāṃ kartṛtvābhimānaśithilībhāvasvarūpāt tanmāhātmyāt tatraiva sthitasya yoginaḥ sarvabhāvādhiṣṭhātṛtvaṃ sarvajñātṛtvaṃ vā samādhir bhavati ||
children.translated_text: Because of that greatness, whose nature is the loosening of the guṇas' presumption of agency, the yogin established there obtains samādhi as lordship over all states or as knowledge of all things.
Lordship over all states is the taking possession, like a master, of all states that are transformations of the guṇas.

children.text: teṣāmeva śāntoditāvyapadeśyadharmatvena sthitānāṃ yathāvad vivekajñānaṃ sarvajñātṛtvam ||
children.translated_text: Knowledge of all things is discriminative knowledge, as they really are, of those same states when they exist as properties that are quiescent, arisen, or not yet nameable.

children.text: eṣā ca asmin śāstre parasyāṃ vaśīkārasaṃjñāyāṃ prāptāyāṃ viśokā nāma siddhir ityucyate ||
children.translated_text: And in this śāstra, when the designation called supreme mastery has been reached, this is called the siddhi named <s>viśokā</s>, 'free from sorrow.'
He next states, in sequence, a further stage.

children.text: tasyām api viśokāyāṃ siddhau yadā vairāgyam utpadyate yoginas tadā tasmād doṣāṇāṃ rāgādīnāṃ yad bījam avidyā tasyāḥ kṣaye nirmūlane kaivalyam ātyantikī duḥkhanivṛttiḥ ||
children.translated_text: Even with regard to that siddhi called <s>viśokā</s>, when detachment arises for the yogin, then from it comes the destruction, the uprooting, of ignorance, which is the seed of defects such as passion; this is <s>kaivalya</s>, the absolute cessation of suffering.
It is the <s>puruṣa</s>'s abiding in its own nature, because the purpose of the guṇas has come to an end.
He states the means of remaining in this very samādhi.
There are four kinds of yogins.
Among them, the first is one possessed of practice, in whom the light has only just begun to operate.
The second is one whose insight is truth-bearing.
The third is one who has conquered the elements and the senses.
The fourth is one who has passed beyond what remains to be cultivated.

children.text: tatra caturthasya samādheḥ prāptasaptavidhaprāntabhūmiprajñasya antyāṃ madhumatīsaṃjñāṃ bhūmiṃ sākṣātkurvataḥ sthānino devā upanimantrayitāro bhavanti divyastrīrasāyanādikam upaḍhaukayanti ||
children.translated_text: For the fourth, whose insight has reached the sevenfold final stages of samādhi and who directly realizes the final stage called <s>madhumatī</s>, the gods who dwell in their stations become inviters and offer divine women, elixirs, and the like.

children.text: tasmin upanimantraṇe nānena saṅgaḥ kartavyaḥ nāpi smayaḥ ||
children.translated_text: With respect to that invitation, he must form neither attachment nor pride.
If he forms attachment, he falls again into enjoyment of sense objects.

children.text: smayakaraṇe kṛtakṛtyam ātmānaṃ manyamāno na samādhāv utsahate ||
children.translated_text: If he forms pride, thinking himself to have accomplished what had to be done, he does not strive in samādhi.
Therefore he must avoid both attachment and pride.

children.text: asyāmeva phalabhūtāyāṃ vivekakhyātau pūrvoktasaṃyamavyatiriktam upāyāntaram āha ||
children.translated_text: In connection with this discriminative discernment, which is the result, he states another means apart from the previously mentioned <s>saṃyama</s>.
A moment is the final, smallest part of time.
Its division cannot be further separated.

children.text: tathāvidhānāṃ kālakṣaṇānāṃ yaḥ kramaḥ paurvāparyeṇa pariṇāmas tatra saṃyamāt prāguktaṃ vivekajaṃ jñānaṃ utpadyate ||
children.translated_text: By <s>saṃyama</s> on the sequence of such moments of time, that is, on their transformation in prior-and-posterior order, the previously mentioned knowledge born of discernment arises.
This is the meaning.

children.text: ayaṃ kālakṣaṇo 'smāt kālakṣaṇāduttaraḥ ayam asmāt pūrva ityevaṃvidhe krame kṛtasaṃyamasyātyantasūkṣme 'pi kṣaṇakrame yadā bhavati sākṣātkāraḥ tadā anyadapi sūkṣmaṃ mahadādi sākṣātkarotīti vivekajñānotpattiḥ ||
children.translated_text: When one who has performed <s>saṃyama</s> on a sequence of this kind, 'this moment of time is later than that moment of time; this one is earlier than that one,' has direct perception even of an extremely subtle sequence of moments, then he directly perceives other subtle things too, beginning with <s>mahat</s>; thus discriminative knowledge arises.
To indicate the specific object of this same <s>saṃyama</s>, he says further.
The causes of distinction among things are class, characteristic, and place.

children.text: kvacidbhedahetur jātiḥ yathā gauriyaṃ mahiṣīyam iti ||
children.translated_text: In some cases class is the cause of distinction, as in, 'this is a cow, this is a buffalo.'

children.text: jātyā tulyayoḥ lakṣaṇaṃ bhedahetuḥ yathā iyaṃ karburā iyam aruṇeti ||
children.translated_text: When two things are the same in class, a characteristic is the cause of distinction, as in, 'this one is speckled, this one is reddish.'

children.text: jātyā lakṣaṇena cābhinnayor bhedahetur deśo dṛṣṭaḥ yathā tulyapramāṇayorāmalakayor bhinnadeśasthitayoḥ ||
children.translated_text: When two things are not distinguished by class or characteristic, place is seen to be the cause of distinction, as in two āmalaka fruits of equal size situated in different places.

children.text: yatra punarbhedo'vadhārayituṃ na śakyate yathaikadeśasthitayoḥ śuklayoḥ pārthivayoḥ paramāṇvoḥ ||
children.translated_text: But where a distinction cannot be determined, as in two white earthy atoms situated in the same place,

children.text: tathāvidhe viṣaye bhedāya kṛtasaṃyamasya yadā bhedena jñānamupajāyate tadā tadabhyāsāt sūkṣmāṇyapi tattvāni bhedena pratipādyante ||
children.translated_text: in such an object, when knowledge arises distinctly for one who has performed <s>saṃyama</s> for the sake of distinction, then through practice of that, even subtle principles are set forth distinctly.

children.text: etad uktaṃ bhavati yatra kenacid upāyena bhedo nāvadhārayituṃ śakyastatra saṃyamādbhavatyeva bhedapratipattiḥ sūkṣmāṇāṃ tattvānāṃ ||
children.translated_text: This is what is meant: where distinction cannot be determined by any means, there distinction of subtle principles certainly arises from <s>saṃyama</s>.

children.text: uktasya vivekajanyajñānasya saṃjñāṃ viṣayaṃ svabhāvyaṃ vyākhyātum āha ||
children.translated_text: He states the designation, object, and nature of the knowledge born of discernment that has been described.
The knowledge produced in the final stage through the power of the stated <s>saṃyama</s> is called <s>tāraka</s>.

children.text: tārayatyagādhāt saṃsārapayodheḥ yoginaṃ ityānvarthikyā saṃjñayā tārakaṃ ityucyate ||
children.translated_text: It is called <s>tāraka</s> by an etymological designation, because it carries the yogin across the unfathomable ocean of <s>saṃsāra</s>.

children.text: asya viṣayamāha sarvaviṣaya iti sarvāṇi tattvāni mahadādīni viṣayo'syeti sarvaviṣayam ||
children.translated_text: He states its object: it has every object, meaning that all principles beginning with <s>mahat</s> are its object.
And its nature is that it has objects in every way.

children.text: sarvvābhiravasthābhiḥ sthūlasūkṣmādibhedena tais taiśca pariṇāmaiḥ sarvveṇākāreṇāvasthitāni tattvāni viṣayo'syeti sarvathāviṣayam ||
children.translated_text: Its object is everything in every way: the principles that are situated in every form, through all states and through their various transformations, distinguished as gross, subtle, and so on.
He states another characteristic.
And it is without sequence.
It is without sequence because there is no succession in its grasping of entities that are one, two, or three, transformed into all the many states without remainder.
The meaning is that it sees everything simultaneously, like an āmalaka fruit in the palm of the hand.
He states what results from this discriminative knowledge, from the knowledge called tāraka.
<s>Sattva</s> and <s>puruṣa</s> are those whose characteristics have been stated.
When the purification of the two is equal, there is <s>kaivalya</s>.
The purification of the mind-sattva is its re-entry into its own cause through the complete cessation of the conceit of agency.
The purification of <s>puruṣa</s> is the absence of experience that has been figuratively attributed to it.

children.text: iti dvayoḥ samānāyāṃ śuddhau puruṣasya kaivalyaṃ utpadyate mokṣo bhavatītyarthaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Thus, when the purification of the two is equal, <s>kaivalya</s> arises for <s>puruṣa</s>; the meaning is that liberation occurs.

children.text: tad evam antaraṅgayogāṅgatrayam abhidhāya tasya ca saṃyamasaṃjñāṃ kṛtvā saṃyamasya viṣayapradarśanārthaṃ pariṇāmatrayamupapādya saṃyamabalotpadyamānāḥ pūrvāntāparāntamadhyabhāvāḥ siddhīrupadarśya samādhyāśvāsotpattaye bāhyā bhuvanajñānādirūpā ābhyantarāśca kāyavyūhajñānādirūpāḥ pradarśya samādhyupayogāyendriyaprāṇādijayapūrvikāḥ pradarśya paramapuruṣārthasiddhaye yathākramam avasthāsahitabhūtajayendriyasattvajayodbhavāśca vyākhyāya vivekajñānotpattaye tāṃstān upāyān upanyasya tārakasya sarvasamādhyavasthāparyantabhavasya svarūpamabhidhāya tatsamāpatteḥ kṛtādhikārasya cittasattvasya svakāraṇānupraveśāt kaivalyamutpadyate ityabhihitaṃ iti vyākṛto vibhutipādaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Thus, having taught the three inner limbs of yoga, having given them the designation <s>saṃyama</s>, having established the three transformations in order to show the objects of <s>saṃyama</s>, having shown the siddhis produced by the power of <s>saṃyama</s> and consisting of states at the prior limit, later limit, and middle, having shown both the external siddhis such as knowledge of the worlds and the internal ones such as knowledge of the arrangement of the body, having shown those preceded by mastery over the senses, vital airs, and so forth for the use of samādhi, having explained in due order the siddhis arising from mastery over the elements together with their states, mastery over the senses, and mastery over sattva, for the accomplishment of the supreme human goal, having set forth various means for the arising of discriminative knowledge, having described the nature of tāraka, which exists up to the final state of all samādhis, it has been stated that, when that attainment has occurred, <s>kaivalya</s> arises through the re-entry into its own cause of the mind-sattva whose function has been fulfilled. Thus the Vibhūtipāda has been explained.
